newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's trade minister orders bureaucrat probe.
newsitem.headline: Japan's trade minister orders bureaucrat probe.

text.p: Japan's trade minister announced on Tuesday an investigation into bureaucratic corruption, the latest in a series of scandals involving civil servants.

The affairs, which in the past week have brought down a deputy health minister and a provincial governor, have put a harsh spotlight on Japan's bureaucrats, once regarded as the backbone of the country's economic success.

Trade Minister Shinji Sato told a news conference that more than 100 high-ranking Ministry of Trade and Industry (MITI) officials would be questioned over links to oil dealer Junichi Izui, who was arrested earlier this month for tax evasion.
"I have given instructions that an investigation be conducted within the ministry of our people's relations with Izui, and for the result to be made public," Sato said.
He said present and past heads of his ministry's Petroleum Department would be among those questioned.

Millionaire oil wholesaler Izui, arrested on charges of evading 310 million yen ($2.76 million) in taxes, has boasted of close ties to high-ranking politicians and bureaucrats who he allegedly wined and dined.
He also donated millions of yen to high-ranking politicians across the political spectrum, including key members in Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's new cabinet.
Investigation of Izui is focusing on some 5.7 billion yen ($50.8 million) in commissions he received for oil transactions involving Mitsubishi Oil and Mitsui Mining Co.

The MITI probe comes a week after the resignation of Vice Health and Welfare Minister Nobuharu Okamitsu, who was implicated in a nursing home construction scandal which has penetrated deep into local and central government.

Japanese media have quoted police as saying that Okamitsu was suspected of receiving more than 60 million yen ($535,000) from an nursing home developer who was arrested recently along with a former senior Health Ministry bureaucrat.

The pair are being held on charges involving millions of yen (dollars) in bribes allegedly paid in order to win hundreds of millions of yen (tens of millions of dollars) in central and provincial government construction subsidies.
Lower down the bureaucrat scale at the local government level, the governor of northern Akita prefecture announced on Monday he would resign because of excesses by local officials.

Kikuji Sasaki's resignation is the first of it's kind at the gubernatorial level. Sakaki said he would step down to take responsibility for massive misuse of taxpayers' money by prefectural government officials.

Some 750 senior bureaucrats acknowledged misusing around 900 million yen ($8.03 million) of taxpayer's money, which they spent on lavish parties or pocketed as expenses for bogus conferences and business trips.
Last month, the vice governor of nearby Miyagi prefecture resigned following similiar revelations involving about 580 million yen ($5.17 million).
The series of civil service scandals is likely to increase pressure on Hashimoto to crackdown on the country's bureaucrats, mainly by cutting their power.
Hashimoto has announced that one of the top priorities of his new government is to reform central government. ($1= 112 yen)
